analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We'll hear arguments next in 74 to 15, United States against Farm. Mr. Tuttle. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court. This case involves the issue of the standards of criminal liability under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act of 1938, as construed by this Court in United States v. Datterwyck and United States v. Weisenfeld Warehouse Company. This is a prosecution of Acme Markets, Inc., and John Park, its president, for holding adulterated food under insanitary conditions in Acme's Baltimore, Maryland warehouse. The corporation, Acme, pleaded guilty prior to trial. Park, the respondent here, was found guilty by a jury after trial. The evidence at trial of adulteration and of insanitary conditions in this case was massive. The FDA inspectors testified at trial that in the basement of the Baltimore warehouse, and this is at page 20 of the record, the inspectors found extensive evidence of rodent infestation in the form of rat and mouse pellets throughout the entire perimeter area and along the wall. On the first floor of the same warehouse, during the same inspection, the inspectors found rodent excreta pellets in the meat-hanging room beside bales of Jell-O and throughout the Jell-O storage area. Not mixed, I know. I'm sorry, Mr. Chief. Jell-O wasn't mixed with it. No. No. Moreover, the inspectors found rodent urine and rodent nesting material in and around food and live and dead rodents throughout the warehouse. Following this inspection, Dr. Norman Kramer of the FDA wrote to Park concerning the conditions of that warehouse. And he told Park, among other things, that the inspectors had found that the warehouse was, quote, actively and extensively inhabited by live rodents. Mr. Kramer added, And such reprehensible conditions obviously existed for a prolonged period of time without detection or were completely ignored. As a follow-up, in March 1972, the FDA conducted a second inspection, and it found some improvement. But it also found evidence of rodent-contaminated food, rodent nesting material, and dead rodents in the warehouse. The evidence at trial respecting Park came from the corporate general counsel, from the bylaws of the corporation, and from Park himself. Mr. Tuttle, what is the essence of the crime charged here? The essence of the crime charged is the holding of food which has become adulterated through the presence of filthy material, which is in the definition of adulteration in the Act, Section 342A3. There is a second violation which is also charged, and that is the holding of food under insanitary conditions whereby it may become adulterated. In order to find Park guilty, the jury would have had to find that he held food in this warehouse? The statute makes it a crime to hold or to... It defines the crime in terms of the causing or the doing or the causing of any of the following acts, and among those is the holding of adulterated food. Adulterated food is then defined in a separate section of the statute, as I have... So it's causing adulterated food to be held... That would be the statutory definition of the crime. Mr. Tuttle, there were fines imposed here, just fines, weren't there? Yes, there were fines imposed against the corporation which pleaded guilty. Park himself was found guilty by the jury of all counts and fined $50 a count for a total of $250 in fines. That's the entire penalty imposed against him individually. Would the government's position be any different if he had been sentenced to jail? No. We would maintain that the statute permits such a disposition. The only difficulty might arise in terms of one might conceivably have more serious due process problems where there was, in fact, incarceration. But in terms of what the statute envisions as a possible disposition, incarceration would be a possibility. I think, in essence, this is an easier case for the court because it simply doesn't raise the problem of incarceration. Why more serious due process problems? Well, I don't believe that there would be insuperable due process problems. Same kind of foundation for a distinction that is illustrated by the Argersinger case, for example. That's a good example where the court held that there had to be counsel where there was going to be any incarceration, but it was sufficiently fair to have a prosecution without counsel where the disposition was a crime merely. Well, really, what you're saying is hard cases make bad law. Well, I'm saying that we don't reach that difficult situation, and I would say that I don't consider it an insuperable problem for the government. I think that there have been criminal penalties imposed under this act, which have included incarceration. Typically, they have involved individuals who had a more intimate involvement with the violation than occurred here. But the statute would certainly permit incarceration. The fact of the matter is that in violations of this sort, district courts are disinclined to impose penalties, including imprisonment, and none were, in fact, imposed in this case. What are the maximum allowable statutory penalties? Well, for a first offender, it carries a maximum allowable penalty of $1,000 or one year in jail. So that possibly he could have been sentenced to jail for five years. Five counts. Five counts, that's right, if he were given consecutive sentences on every count. Again, that's not what happened, and I don't think it presents the problem that this court need resolve at this juncture. I was speaking about the evidence respecting Park himself in the case. The bylaws of the corporation give Park general and active supervision of the affairs, business, offices, and employees of the company. Park himself took the stand and acknowledged his responsibility in sanitation matters. He said, Sanitation, quote, Is a thing I am responsible for in the entire operation of the company. More generally, Park said, I was about to quote him on everything else in the company, Mr. Justice. He said, Actually, I am responsible for the entire organizational structure of the company. And he went on to say that for any result that occurs in the company, I am ultimately the chief executive officer and therefore responsible. I think that his particular responsibilities with respect to sanitation were an important element of the government's proof at trial, including the notice that he had received of prior violations and the notice that he received of the first four violations involved in this charge. Is this the principal part of your case, I take it, that he was president and the president has responsibility? Absolutely. That is a principal part of the case. The essence of the responsibility that he has lies in his duties under the bylaws and his powers to deal with the problem that the law defines. And you rely on Dottowicz? We rely, we find this case governed by Dottowicz, as did, I should say, the trial court. Anything that corporation could be convicted for, I take it then that Park could be? Under the Food and Drug Act, yes. Or any other crime, or any other crime, if that's what the law is. Well, it would depend, of course, on the nature of the crime. If that's what the criminal law says. Well, if that's what the criminal law says. But the fact is that the Food and Drug Act is rather a specific piece of legislation creating, we believe, special duties on people who deal in foods and drugs. Well, you must say that the president of the company can be held to have committed this crime because he's president. Well, but many, many criminal laws require sci-enter, as this law does not. Now, in that case, the corporation might be guilty by virtue of the knowing conduct of some subordinate other than the president. The president would not be guilty because he would not have the knowledge which would be an element of the offense. Our case rests almost entirely on the special nature of these laws. What would be the constitutional violation if they had indicted you for this crime? You would just say, well, I didn't do it. I mean, I wasn't there. I'm not responsible. I couldn't even connect with the corporation, I suppose. You'd just say it's... Of course I would. The difference between you and Farmer is the president of the company. And I had no responsibility with respect to that problem. The law imposed no duty on me. I'm not in the business. I didn't undertake to go into the business of handling dangerous drugs, dangerous medical devices, or food. I simply have... The law has not laid that obligation upon me and consequently can't hold me responsible if a problem occurs in ACME. Well, let's bring it closer to this situation. Suppose it was the vice president in charge of sales. They'd have a rather difficult time making a case out against him, wouldn't they? Well, that would, of course, depend upon the organizational structure of the business and his responsibilities. I was assuming that the normal function of a sales vice president is to see that the goods are sold and not how they're produced particularly. I would agree. We would have to discuss what the function of it was. But if one spoke about the accountant or the lawyer for the corporation, in-house lawyer, who had no responsibilities in the organizational structure for this problem, then he would probably not hold a responsible relation to the violation. Now, the concept of the responsible relation I want to develop later in my argument because it is the essence of what Dottorweick teaches the jury must find in order to find an individual responsible for a violation. The chief executive officer, unless it's in a very unusual situation, is always going to have a responsible relation. If he happens to be the chief executive officer of a company that makes or warehouses products subject to the food and drug act. I would say, except in the most unusual situation, he would be in a responsible relation. One could conceive... By definition, or ipso facto, whatever you mean. If he was not, it would be by virtue of some kind of limitations on his power, which would have placed the power somewhere else, in a general manager or some other person who was the apex of... The chief executive officer of the corporation, and if the corporation can be found guilty, as my brother White says, then inevitably he, so can he be, if he is, in fact, the chief executive officer. Mr. Justice, I agree with that, subject to the limitation that we have to look at laws of this kind. Yes, but that is the argument in this case. We're talking about the food and drug, these food and drug laws. Yes. That's as much of the concept of responsibilities you need in this case. You don't need to develop it any new. That's the end of it. Well, that would be a sufficient basis for the sending of the case to the jury. I do think that the line of command and the relationship that the individual has to the violation or to the prohibited conditions is something that the government would ordinarily want to show in its case in chief because the question is committed to the jury on the instruction that if the individual is to be found guilty, it will be by virtue of his responsible relation to the problem, which would be his... He's a chief executive officer of the corporation. He inevitably has a responsibility with relation to that problem or any other corporate problem. I would say in most instances, it might be, as Mr. Justice, you are aware, in the Weisenfeld decision, you adumbrated a possibility that a corporate executive... Well, that was a case, of course, involving a corporation, but raised for us the suggestion that there might be situations where the corporate executive, be he someone lower in the chain of command, or the chief executive might be powerless to deal with a problem, and that might be a matter of affirmative defense that he could assert.
